overview: This week's papers cluster around how systems learn and use the statistics of their environment. One account shows that [comprehenders' error corrections track real production error rates](#p6) for subject-verb agreement, and a large-scale eye-tracking analysis finds that [the word frequency effect shrinks but persists](#p4) even for highly predictable words, which favors interactive accounts over independent-factor models. A related discourse study finds that [connectives speed reading beyond what relation, content, or form predictions explain](#p7), so integration seems to matter alongside prediction. On attention, [working-memory and long-term-memory templates](#p1) appear to feed one shared priority signal, since responses to targets matching both colors beat the race model bound. [Children as young as 5-6](#p3) also show learned suppression of a salient colored distractor, with no clear age difference. Among the modeling papers, [a Lévy-flight account of evidence accumulation](#p2) fit better than diffusion variants, with heavier-tailed noise giving way to more Gaussian-like noise under time pressure. [Simulations of collaborative recognition](#p0) show that groups can outperform their best member, but only under certain conditions. And [language models learning statistical structure without weight updates](#p5) challenge the assumption that adaptation requires plasticity.

papers.title: A REM Model of Collaborative Recognition Memory
papers.authors: Yiyan Tan, Richard M. Shiffrin, Timothy J. Pleskac
papers.summary: Many recognition decisions are made by groups, so this work builds a model (CO-REM) on top of the REM model of individual recognition and compares ways of combining memory: sharing old/new calls, sharing confidence, or pooling the raw memory evidence. In simulations, groups can beat even their best member, but only under certain conditions, such as how similar members' abilities are and how evidence is shared. Confidence sharing can help or hurt depending on how people map evidence onto confidence. The model also predicts bigger group gains for studied items than for correctly rejecting new ones, though the differences are small.
papers.abstract: Recognition memory is often studied as an individual process, yet many recognition decisions are made collaboratively. Collaborative recognition requires individuals to communicate and combine separate, imperfect memory evidence to reach a joint decision. Here, we develop a computational model of collaborative recognition memory (CO-REM) grounded in the well-established Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model of individual recognition. We compare collaborative decision rules based on categorical old/new decisions, confidence judgments, and the direct integration of memory evidence. The simulations show that groups can outperform even their best individual member, but the benefits depend on differences in individual recognition ability and how memory evidence is communicated and combined. Confidence sharing can produce collective gains or losses depending on how individuals map their memory evidence onto confidence judgments. The model also predicts greater collaborative benefits for recognizing previously studied items (targets) than for correctly rejecting new items (lures), consistent with some previous empirical findings. Although the predicted performance differences are small, CO-REM provides a framework for identifying the conditions under which collaboration improves recognition and for guiding future empirical investigations.

papers.title: Working- and long-term memory target templates converge to produce coactive guidance of attention during visual search
papers.authors: Brett Bahle, Zexuan Niu, Jeremy Strueder et al.
papers.summary: People searched for a target defined by either of two cued colors, one changing every trial (held in working memory) and one fixed (held in long-term memory). Dynamic-match targets were found more efficiently than static-match ones, yet when a target matched both colors, response times were faster than two independent parallel guidance processes could produce, a violation of the race model inequality. That pattern points to working-memory and long-term-memory templates feeding into one shared attentional priority signal, even though they are maintained in quite different ways.
papers.abstract: Templates that guide attention during visual search can be maintained in visual working memory (VWM) or in long-term memory (LTM). A central challenge for theories of attention is explaining how these sources of bias combine to determine selection. Here, we tested whether they converge on a common priority signal. Specifically, we contrasted a coactive model of guidance, assuming convergence, with three non-coactive alternatives, each holding that guidance from VWM and LTM operate independently. Participants searched for the presence of a target defined by either of two cued colors. One cued color changed on each trial (dynamic, engaging VWM), whereas the other remained constant (static, engaging LTM). The target could match either one of the cued colors (single-target trials) or both (redundant-target trials). Through distributional analysis, we tested for the presence of redundant-target RTs that were faster than could have been generated by the two individual guidance processes operating independently in parallel. Such "violations" of the race model inequality (RMI) are observed only within a coactive system. For single-target trials, searches were substantially more efficient for dynamic-match targets than for static-match targets. Nevertheless, we observed robust violations of the RMI on redundant-target trials. Together, these results demonstrate that target templates can be maintained in qualitatively different states yet ultimately converge to jointly influence a common attentional priority signal.

papers.title: Time to jump: Exploring the distribution of noise in evidence accumulation as a function of time pressure
papers.authors: Julia V. Liss, Mischa von Krause, Lasse Elsemüller et al.
papers.summary: The Lévy-flight model loosens the diffusion model's assumption of Gaussian noise, allowing occasional big jumps in evidence accumulation, and its α parameter controls how heavy-tailed those jumps are. Across two experiments (N = 341 and N = 160) with letter-number and brightness discrimination, the Lévy model fit better than diffusion variants, and α dropped as time pressure rose, especially under an explicit 500 ms deadline where RT distributions became nearly symmetrical. Modeling the timeout also sharply lowered diffusion drift rates but changed the Lévy model's only modestly. Fitting relied on BayesFlow, a deep-learning approach to simulation-based inference, because the model's likelihood can't be computed directly.
papers.abstract: The diffusion model conceptualizes binary decisions as emerging from continuous evidence accumulation with Gaussian noise. The Lévy-flight model (LFM) extends this by allowing accumulation noise to follow a heavier-tailed distribution, enabling sudden, large jumps in evidence accumulation. The heavy-tailedness is governed by the stability parameter α, with smaller α-values indicating more frequent and larger jumps. We demonstrate through simulation that the LFM can generate near-symmetrical response time (RT) distributions typical under strict deadlines. In Study 1, we explored the influence of intense time pressure on α in a letter-number discrimination task, expecting higher time pressure to entail smaller α-values. Participants (N = 341) were assigned to an accuracy (unlimited RT), implicit deadline (feedback discouraging RTs over 500 ms), or explicit deadline condition (timeout at 500 ms). Given the LFM's intractable likelihood, we used BayesFlow, a framework for simulation-based inference with deep learning. Model comparisons consistently favored the LFM over diffusion model variants-even in the accuracy condition. Importantly, α-values decreased with increasing time pressure and were especially low in the explicit deadline condition, where RT distributions also approached symmetry. Estimating both the LFM and a structurally matched diffusion model, with and without timeout modeling, further showed that accounting for timeout-related RT truncation led to substantially lower diffusion model drift rates, whereas LFM drift rates changed only modestly. Study 2 (N = 160) replicated α's sensitivity to time pressure in a brightness discrimination task. Overall, α responded systematically to temporal constraints across both tasks and timeout modeling specifications.

papers.title: Children can suppress salient distractors.
papers.authors: Aniruddha Ramgir, Keerthana Kapiley, Dominique Lamy
papers.summary: Can 5-6 and 8-9 year olds learn to ignore a distracting color? Children searched for a shape-defined target while a uniquely colored distractor appeared on most trials, with its color changing each block. Interference from the distractor shrank in the second half of blocks, once the color was familiar, and this happened similarly in both age groups. Feature-based suppression therefore seems to be in place by age 5-6, consistent with implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms.
papers.abstract: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5-6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5-6 and 8-9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor's color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5-6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. papers.title: Revisiting the interaction between word frequency and predictability in natural reading: Large-scale evidence based on large language models
papers.authors: Xiaoxuan Li, Bernhard Angele, Baoguo Chen
papers.summary: Using an ensemble of large language models to estimate how predictable each word is, this work analyzed six eye-tracking datasets of natural reading in English and Chinese. The word frequency effect shrank as predictability rose but didn't vanish even for highly predictable words. That fits interactive accounts where context-driven preactivation eases lexical access without replacing it, and it conflicts with eye-movement models that treat frequency and predictability as independent, though those could probably be adapted.
papers.abstract: Word predictability-that is, the predictability of a word in a sentence based on the preceding context-reliably influences processing of that word. Prior research has consistently reported additive effects of word predictability and frequency, suggesting that contextual influence may operate independently of bottom-up lexical access. We leveraged an ensemble of large language models (LLMs) to derive predictability estimates across six natural reading eye-tracking datasets in English and Chinese. Across both languages, we found that the frequency effect was attenuated with increasing word probability yet remained significant under the high predictability conditions. These findings support the interactive processing account and Chinese Reading Model, which assume that top-down preactivation reduces the demand for bottom-up lexical access, but does not fully replace it. The findings are inconsistent with the independent relationship implemented in some other computational models of eye-movement control. However, such models could readily be extended to accommodate this interaction.

papers.title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning
papers.authors: Gili Lior, Yuval Shalev, Gabriel Stanovsky et al.
papers.summary: A common assumption is that adapting to new tasks requires changing the learning system's connections, as with neural plasticity. Here, large language models were tested on statistical learning tasks involving arbitrary word sequences, and they picked up the underlying structures without any weight updates, even though these were far from their training distribution. The argument is that a sufficiently trained system can adapt through computation alone, more than has usually been acknowledged. It also suggests deep learning models as a source of hypotheses about the brain.
papers.abstract: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, even though these structures carry no semantic content and lie far from the natural language distribution on which the models were trained. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

papers.title: Comprehenders' Error Correction Mechanisms Are Finely Calibrated to Language Production Statistics
papers.authors: Peng Qian, Roger Levy
papers.summary: If readers correct errors using a noisy-channel model of how speakers produce language, that model should be tuned to how often different mistakes actually happen. To test this, participants edited sentences containing subject-verb agreement mismatches to say what they thought was meant, since production error rates for these are estimable. Bayesian analysis showed their corrections reflected both item-specific prior expectations and structure-sensitive error likelihoods that closely tracked real production error rates. Comprehenders appear to track the statistics of their linguistic environment quite finely.
papers.abstract: An essential feature of human communication is robustness to errors: even when speakers and writers make mistakes, listeners and readers can usually determine the intended meaning. A leading hypothesis is that comprehenders achieve robust error correction by internally deploying a “noisy‐channel” model of the language production process. Crucially, to best achieve error robustness, a comprehender's noisy‐channel model should be finely calibrated to the environmental statistics of language production, incorporating not only prior expectations about communicative intents but also structure‐sensitive likelihoods of different types of speaker error. This environmentally calibrated noisy‐channel hypothesis has been difficult to test, because the rates of most types of language production errors are hard to estimate. Here, we test this hypothesis by experimentally investigating comprehenders' interpretations of subject–verb agreement errors, for which context‐contingent language production error rates are feasible to estimate. In a novel free‐form error correction task, participants edited sentences with subject–verb agreement mismatches to indicate what they think was intended. Bayesian analysis of the resulting data shows that comprehenders' interpretations reflect both item‐specific prior expectations and structure‐sensitive error likelihoods that closely correspond to error rates in language production. These results provide quantitative evidence that humans closely track prior statistics over linguistic forms and deploy a noisy‐channel model finely calibrated to statistics of the linguistic environment to achieve robust language understanding.

papers.title: Comprehenders’ Expectations During Discourse Processing: Disentangling Relation, Content, and Form Predictions From Connective Facilitation
papers.authors: Marian Marchal, Merel Scholman, Ted Sanders et al.
papers.summary: Predictions in discourse can concern the relation type, the meaning, or the exact wording, and these usually get confounded. Here they were separated using a continuation task plus self-paced reading and eye-tracking experiments. Connectives raised relation-type predictability and in turn content predictability, and relation-type predictability affected reading times only indirectly, via content predictability; it even came with longer initial reading times in the eye-tracking study. Connectives sped reading even after accounting for all three kinds of predictability, so their benefit goes beyond prediction, which suggests both predictive and integrative processes matter.
papers.abstract: Comprehenders have been shown to make predictions about upcoming information at multiple levels, but the role of prediction in the processing of discourse relations remains unclear. This study investigated the role of prediction in discourse relation processing by disentangling three levels of predictability which are typically confounded: relation type, semantic content, and lexical-syntactic form. Furthermore, connectives are known to facilitate reading of subsequent material; here we examine whether this effect can be explained by connectives enhancing predictability at multiple levels, or whether they exert processing benefits beyond their effects on prediction. We derive measures of relation type, content predictability, and form predictability from a continuation task (Exp. 1) and show that the presence of a connective increases the predictability of the relation type and, in turn, of the semantic content. In a self-paced reading (Exp. 2) and an eye-tracking experiment (Exp. 3), we find that relation type predictability is indirectly associated with reading times through content predictability. However, relation type predictability did not directly facilitate processing and was associated with longer initial reading times in Exp. 3, suggesting that its effects on processing may be more complex than straightforward facilitation. The connective showed direct effects on reading times even after controlling for all three levels of predictability, suggesting that connective facilitation operates through mechanisms beyond enhanced prediction. These findings support accounts in which predictions at different linguistic levels constrain one another and show that both predictive and integrative mechanisms contribute to discourse comprehension.

papers.title: Computations of Contingency Guide How Experience is Summarized in Memory
papers.authors: Anna Leshinskaya, Sharon L. Thompson-Schill
papers.summary: Memory for pairs of events seems to follow contingency (ΔP) rather than plain conditional probability. That means how strongly A and B are linked depends not just on how often A is followed by B, but also on how often B occurs without A. Participants' memory after incidental exposure matched ΔP, and the effect could come from strong competing predictors or a high base rate of the outcome. An adapted Rescorla-Wagner model captured the results, linking statistical learning to classical conditioning.
papers.abstract: The human mind spontaneously summarizes experience into predictive models by encoding regularities across individual observations. However, there is a variety of possible ways it may do so, and diverse models of this process have been proposed in different learning paradigms. Here, we bridge the tradition of statistical learning (SL) with that of classical conditioning to show that memory formation, not just anticipatory behavior, follows the principle of contingency or ΔP. We showed that participants' memory for pairwise predictive regularities reflects contingency rather than conditional probability, as often assumed. By this principle, the relationship between stimulus pairs A and B is a function not only of how often A is followed by B, but also how often B occurs without A. We showed that ΔP captures what participants remember about event pairs after exposure, revealing that this principle indeed guides how experience is summarized into models in memory during incidental encoding. We additionally showed that this effect can arise either from strong competing predictors or an overall high base rate of the outcome. An adapted version of the Rescorla Wagner learning model captured these findings, indicating a continuity between SL and many other forms of learning.

papers.title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
papers.authors: Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu et al.
papers.summary: To make multimodal language models reason more like people, this work builds on a behavior-derived space of 66 interpretable dimensions drawn from 4.70 million human odd-one-out judgments. For each triplet, the most salient dimension is turned into a linguistic rationale, so the model learns both the choice and a human-like justification. The models agreed more with human similarity judgments while staying competitive on standard multimodal benchmarks, and they showed greater representational alignment with human fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.

papers.title: An Algorithmic Account of Few-Shot Concept Induction in Language Models
papers.authors: Michael A. Lepori, Laila Johnston, Aalok Sathe et al.
papers.summary: How do language models figure out which features of examples matter when inferring a concept from just a few positives? The proposed hypothesis, Amortized Direction Accentuation, says the model summarizes the examples in a feature space already shaped by prior knowledge of which features usually help find commonalities. The authors tested it in language models on a few-shot concept induction task and report that it holds up. The idea is offered as an account of contextualization in models and as a possible hypothesis about cognition.
papers.abstract: Both models and minds not only encode features that describe an entity, but can specifically represent which features of that entity are relevant for a given context. This core capability underlies in-context learning in language models and a variety of cognitive phenomena in minds, yet it is unclear how intelligent systems identify and promote relevant features. In this work, we propose Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA), an algorithmic hypothesis that provides an explanation for how relevance is determined in the context of few-shot concept induction --- the ability to infer a latent concept from a small number of positive examples. Under ADA, concept induction proceeds by forming a summary representation of the examples in a feature space that is shaped by amortized knowledge about which features tend to be useful for finding commonalities between items. We investigate and validate ADA in language models using a few-shot concept induction task. This work provides a novel perspective on the mechanisms supporting contextualization in language models and a promising hypothesis for a core aspect of cognition.

papers.title: Quantifying metacognition with the hmetad package in R
papers.authors: Kevin O'Neill, Stephen M Fleming
papers.summary: The meta-d' model is a popular way to measure metacognitive sensitivity and bias within signal detection theory, but it's awkward to apply to longitudinal, repeated-measures, or other complex designs. This paper introduces hmetad, an open-source R package that fits the model across many designs using familiar formula syntax. It also walks through validating the model in a Bayesian workflow by examining posterior estimates, and provides tools for evaluating and visualizing fits.
papers.abstract: A longstanding goal in metacognition research is the quantification of confidence-related parameters independently from task performance. While there is now a proliferation of generative models of confidence in numerous psychological tasks, the meta-d' model remains a popular approach to estimating metacognitive sensitivity and metacognitive bias within a signal detection theoretic framework. However, as questions in metacognition research increase in complexity, it remains an ongoing challenge to develop extensions of the meta-d' model built to deal with longitudinal, repeated-measures, or other complex experimental designs. Here we introduce the open-source R package hmetad, which allows users to fit the meta-d' model for a wide range of experimental designs using a familiar formula syntax. We also review how the meta-d' model can be validated in a Bayesian workflow which investigates posterior estimates of key parameters. Overall, the hmetad package offers a comprehensive interface to fitting, evaluating, and visualizing signal detection theoretic models of metacognition.

papers.title: The Temporal Trajectory of Visual Perspective in Autobiographical Memory
papers.authors: Nilay Ozdemir Haksever, Peggy L. St. Jacques
papers.summary: Across 18,229 autobiographical memories from 80 participants, memory age in days was used to track how visual perspective changes over time. Observer-like perspectives rose and own-eyes perspectives fell along a negatively accelerated curve, with the sharpest change among recent memories; about half of the modeled shift occurred within four months, though change continued over years. Stronger reliving and emotional intensity dampened the shifts, and rehearsal also moderated them. The first months after an event look especially dynamic for how memories are visualized.
papers.abstract: Autobiographical memories differ systematically with remoteness, yet little is known about the temporal form of these differences or when they are most pronounced. One consistent change over time concerns visual perspective—as memories become more remote, own-eyes perspectives become less prominent and observer-like perspectives more prominent. Because visual perspective specifies the vantage point from which a remembered event is mentally seen, these shifts may reflect changes in how visual imagery of past events is reconstructed over time. We examined the temporal trajectory of visual perspective across 18,229 autobiographical memories from 80 participants, using memory age measured in days to characterize its relationship with own-eyes and observer-like perspectives at a finer temporal resolution than in previous work. For both perspectives, age-related differences followed a negatively accelerated trajectory. Observer perspective increased and own-eyes perspective decreased most sharply among relatively recent memories, with progressively smaller differences at greater memory ages. Approximately half of the total modeled difference occurred within the first four months, although the trajectory continued across several years. Higher reliving and emotional intensity were associated with attenuated age-related shifts in both perspectives, and rehearsal also moderated their trajectories. These findings show that visual perspective varies nonlinearly across autobiographical memory age and identify the early months after an event as a particularly dynamic period. More broadly, the results characterize the temporal organization of autobiographical imagery, linking the viewpoint from which past events are visualized to both their remoteness and the subjective qualities of recollection.

papers.title: Image size effect on memory generalizes to deeper encoding and cannot be explained by perceptual measures
papers.authors: Shaimaa Masarwa, Olga Kreichman, Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
papers.summary: Earlier work found larger images are better remembered under incidental encoding, and three experiments (n = 189) asked whether that holds with deeper encoding and whether it's just a perception issue. Memory improved with image size under naturalistic, intentional, and perceptual encoding tasks, even though perceptual performance was at ceiling for all sizes. So smaller images aren't simply seen worse; image size seems to shape memory encoding directly, pointing to a role for low-level visual properties.
papers.abstract: We have recently found that during shallow (“naturalistic”/incidental) encoding larger images are better remembered. However, it is unclear whether this reflects a genuine influence of image size on mnemonic processes or an epiphenomenal consequence of its influence on perception, and whether this effect robustly generalizes to deeper encoding. Here, we tested these in three experiments (n = 189) differing in encoding depth: naturalistic (freely viewing the images without being informed a memory test will follow), intentional memorization (freely viewing while memorizing the images since a memory test was to follow), or perceptual encoding (reporting for each image whether there was a person in it and whether it was taken indoors or outdoors, without being informed a memory test will follow). During encoding in the perceptual experiment, participants viewed 160 images of different sizes (3°-15.5°) followed by an old-new recognition memory test of 320 images (half “old”). While perceptual measures were at ceiling, memory improved with image size, presenting a dissociation between perception and memory and indicating that the effect of image size on memory is not a mere reflection of limited perception for smaller images. Additionally, the effect of image size on memory generalized to all encoding tasks such that memory improved for larger images (as evident by accuracy and d’), regardless of average memory performance increasing with encoding depth. These findings suggest that image size operates as a genuine sensory-based modulator of memory encoding, beyond perceptual sensitivity, pointing to a broader role of low-level visual properties in shaping memory representations.

papers.title: No Memory Needed? Perceptual Matching Accounts for a Large Part of the Working Memory–Intelligence Link
papers.authors: Gidon T. Frischkorn, Klaus Oberauer, Alessandra S. Souza
papers.summary: The usual explanation for the link between working memory capacity and fluid intelligence is that both depend on maintaining information. Here, a perceptual matching task with no maintenance demand was added in two studies (N = 346 and N = 267), and matching accuracy strongly predicted fluid intelligence and accounted for a large share of the shared variance with working memory capacity. Maintenance still explained some unique variance in intelligence beyond matching. The results suggest a shared signal-to-noise factor affecting perception, working memory, and intelligence, alongside a specific role for maintenance.
papers.abstract: Working memory capacity (WMC) and fluid intelligence (Gf) are strongly correlated, usually attributed to shared demands on WM maintenance. We test this account against an alternative: shared representational quality. We included an experimentally controlled simplification of visual WM tasks – a perceptual matching task without maintenance demands – alongside WMC and Gf measures. Study 1 (N = 346; younger and older adults) used color and orientation stimuli; Study 2 (N = 267; younger adults) added luminance matching and a broader WMC battery. Matching accuracy strongly predicted Gf and accounted for a large share of the WMC–Gf covariance. WM maintenance accounted for unique Gf variance over and above matching in all groups. These findings are consistent with a shared signal-to-noise ratio affecting perceptual discrimination, WMC, and Gf. They question the view that the WMC–Gf relationship reflects only demands on WM maintenance, while confirming a specific role of maintenance for Gf.

papers.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
papers.authors: Jason Geller
papers.summary: Participants answered prequestions about polio or tuberculosis (or neither) and then read a text on both topics while their eyes were tracked, so every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Memory and eye movements both improved only for the prequestioned information. Typical reading time for the answer sentences didn't change. Instead, those sentences got more unusually long readings, more look-backs, and longer re-reading, which suggests prequestions don't boost attention across the board but trigger extra processing when readers recognize an answer.
papers.abstract: Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information theyaddress, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention tothat information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read atext about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so thatevery target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improvedmemory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the samespecificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusuallylong readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attentionselectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readersrecognize an answer.

papers.title: Depth of Processing and Congruency Interact to Shape Electrophysiological Signatures of Recognition Memory
papers.authors: Martín García-Montes, David Ferrera, Dino Soldic et al.
papers.summary: In this EEG study, 36 young adults did a recognition task after either shallow perceptual or deep semantic encoding, with congruency with existing knowledge varied separately. Deep encoding gave better performance and a larger late positive component, a marker of recollection, while congruency had no effect on either. Congruency did change the earlier FN400 response, though, and mostly after shallow encoding, so early and late stages of recognition seem to depend on different things.
papers.abstract: Recognition memory is influenced by both the depth of processing during encoding and the congruency of incoming information with existing knowledge. Although both factors have been shown to affect memory performance, their combined influence on the electrophysiological mechanisms underlying recognition remains unclear. The present study investigated how level of processing (LOP) and semantic congruency interact to modulate behavioral performance and event-related potentials (ERPs) associated with recognition memory. Thirty-six healthy young adults completed a recognition task in which encoding required either shallow perceptual judgments or deep semantic judgments, while congruency was manipulated independently. Behavioral performance was assessed using Linear Integrated Speed–Accuracy Scores (LISAS), and ERP components were identified through temporo-spatial principal component analysis. Deep encoding produced significantly better behavioral performance and larger late positive component (LPC) amplitudes than shallow encoding, indicating enhanced recollection-related processing. In contrast, semantic congruency did not significantly influence behavioral performance or LPC activity. However, congruency strongly modulated the FN400 component, with incongruent items eliciting more negative responses than congruent items. Importantly, this effect interacted with depth of processing, such that congruency-related differences were pronounced following shallow encoding but attenuated following deep encoding. These findings suggest a functional dissociation between early and late stages of recognition memory. While recollection-related activity appears to be primarily driven by goaldirected semantic processing, early neural responses are sensitive to the interaction between encoding demands and schema compatibility. The results support accounts proposing that recognition memory emerges from the dynamic interplay between mismatch detection and semantic integration processes.

papers.title: Assessing conditionals: An experimental comparison of suppositional and inferential accounts
papers.authors: Alessandro Bogani, Andrea Iacona, Stefania Pighin et al.
papers.summary: There are two ways to say when an 'if...then' statement is acceptable: by the probability of the consequent given the antecedent (suppositional), or by how much the antecedent supports the consequent (inferential). Across three experiments using a new procedure designed to pull these predictions apart, most people's judgments followed one of the normative accounts. Which one depended on the conditional type: arbitrary links like 'if the toy is a triangle, it's yellow' fit the suppositional account, while causal links fit the inferential one.
papers.abstract: Two main normative accounts have been proposed to explain the acceptability of a conditional. The suppositional account equates acceptability with the probability of the consequent given the antecedent, whereas the inferential account maintains that it depends on the support the antecedent provides to the consequent. Previous empirical work has addressed the descriptive accuracy of normative and non-normative accounts, but the results have been inconclusive. In the present study, we introduce a novel experimental procedure designed to dissociate the predictions of competing accounts and employ it in three experiments. Overall, the results indicate that most individuals endorse a normative interpretation of conditionals; however, the specific account that best captures their judgments depends on the type of conditional evaluated. For conditionals in which the antecedent and the consequent stand in an arbitrary relation (e.g., “If the toy is a triangle, then it will be yellow”), judgments align more closely with the suppositional account. In contrast, for conditionals where the antecedent and the consequent are directly causally related (e.g., “If the laser is misaligned, then the prosthesis will have cracks” or “If the prosthesis has cracks, then the laser was misaligned”), judgments are better captured by the inferential account. Possible extensions of current models aimed at achieving a comprehensive characterization of conditionals are briefly discussed.

papers.title: An orthographic advantage in spoken word recognition: Behavioral and ERP evidence from cross- and within-modal priming in Korean
papers.authors: Joonwoo Kim, Solbin Lee, Kichun Nam
papers.summary: Korean Hangul keeps spelling constant even when pronunciation shifts, so the researchers could test whether a prime matching a word's written first syllable helps more than one matching its actual spoken first syllable. In two EEG experiments with auditory lexical decision (spoken primes in one, visual primes in the other), spelling-matched primes sped responses and improved accuracy more than sound-matched ones. The spelling advantage was bigger with visual primes, and orthographic relatedness also showed up in the N400 window. The takeaway is that spelling plays a role in recognizing spoken words, and more surface overlap doesn't automatically mean more help.
papers.abstract: Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation. Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target’s written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2). In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes. The O–P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes. Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming. Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350–550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference. Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250–350 ms window, more than following auditory primes. The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established. The behavioral O–P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference. The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.

papers.title: High-dimensional hippocampus representation facilitates learning of low-dimensional abstract representation and supports generalization
papers.authors: Wang, B., Johnston, W. J., Fusi, S.
papers.summary: This is a modeling paper on a puzzle: the hippocampus uses high-dimensional, sparse codes, yet semantic knowledge seems to live in low-dimensional abstract formats in cortex. Treating the hippocampus as a sparse, decorrelating autoencoder feeding a downstream network like prefrontal cortex, the authors show it helps abstract representations form reliably and efficiently, especially when inputs and desired outputs are poorly aligned. Consolidating hippocampal representations into a separate pathway also improved generalization, so the hippocampus's high-dimensional code ends up supporting abstraction rather than competing with it.
papers.abstract: Semantic knowledge encompasses facts, concepts, and their relationships. Recent work has proposed that some forms of semantic knowledge could be encoded in low-dimensional neural representations, such as the abstract, disentangled representational geometries observed in many cognitive brain areas. Experimental work has shown that hippocampal (HPC) lesions impair the formation of flexible and generalizable semantic knowledge. However, HPC representations are often high-dimensional and sparse. How can these representations contribute to the formation of low-dimensional abstract representation across these cognitive cortical areas? Here, we reconcile these observations using multiregional neural network models. Modeling HPC as a sparse, decorrelating autoencoder, we show that its high-dimensional representations promote the robust and efficient formation of low-dimensional abstract representations in downstream regions such as prefrontal cortex. This effect is most pronounced when the geometry of sensory inputs is misaligned with the geometry of desired outputs, requiring a more complex input-output transformation. Mathematical analysis shows that hippocampal expansion recoding suppresses misleading low-dimensional input structure and reshapes the loss landscape of downstream networks, allowing abstract semantic geometry to emerge reliably. The resulting abstract representations provide an inductive bias for sample-efficient learning of novel semantic-to-action mappings. Finally, we show that consolidating hippocampus-dependent representations into a hippocampus-independent pathway improves out-of-distribution generalization based on input structure. Together, these results suggest a circuit mechanism by which high-dimensional hippocampal representations can support, rather than oppose, the emergence of low-dimensional abstract representations.

papers.title: General versus specific: Investigating the structure of individual differences in post-error slowing across time
papers.authors: Clifford E. Hauenstein, Eunbee Kim, Alexis Phillips et al.
papers.summary: Slowing down after an error is well studied on average, but less is known about why people differ in it. Using latent variable modeling on two large samples who did three inhibitory control tasks, the researchers found that individual differences reflect both a general ability shared across tasks and task-specific ones. The general factor seemed to matter less as time passed after the error.
papers.abstract: Erroneous actions are typically followed by behavioral slowing, known as post-error slowing (PES), along with other post-error adjustments. These effects emerge on the first trial following an error and can persist across subsequent trials. While PES has been extensively studied experimentally, less attention has been given to inter-individual variability. Evidence suggests that the mechanisms underlying individual differences in PES are largely domain-general, spanning multiple tasks. However, as time elapses from the point of error, task-specific processes may increasingly influence these individual differences. In this study, we applied latent variable modeling to two large samples of participants who completed three canonical inhibitory control paradigms. Our findings indicate that individual differences in PES reflect both domain-general and task-specific abilities, with the influence of the domain-general factor seeming to decrease over time following error commission.

papers.title: The emergence of language-specific biases in visual attention in pre-reading toddlers from two cultures
papers.authors: Christine E. Potter, Nadeen Kherbawy, Christopher R. Sepulveda et al.
papers.summary: Toddlers aged 2.5 to 4 who couldn't yet read named pictured objects in a picture naming task, and the direction they went in matched their language's writing direction. Hebrew-learning children labeled objects right to left, while English- and Spanish-learning children did the opposite, and the tendencies grew stronger with age. So cultural conventions seem to shape attention well before any reading instruction.
papers.abstract: Skilled adult readers show biases in their visual attention that reflect the direction of their native writing systems (e.g., English readers scan left-to-right while Hebrew readers scan right-to-left), but it not yet clear when these biases develop. We tested the hypothesis that language-specific patterns of behavior precede the ability to read by testing how toddlers (2.5-4 years) exposed to different writing systems allocated their attention in a picture naming task. Across two communities, children tended to name objects in the direction that matched their native language. Hebrew-learning toddlers labeled objects from right-to-left, while English- and Spanish-learning toddlers showed the reverse pattern, and language-specific tendencies strengthened with age. These results demonstrate that children have begun to discover directional regularities associated with their language even before they receive literacy instruction and illustrate how cultural conventions exert a direct influence on children's attention from a very young age.

papers.title: Universal patterns in the acquisition of negation and disjunction: Parallels between L1 and L2
papers.authors: Elena Pagliarini, Jin Yan, Anna Gavarró
papers.summary: Adult second-language learners, with Mandarin or Spanish as their native language, interpreted sentences like 'John didn't eat the cucumber or the pepper'. Native speakers preferred the 'not both' reading, while learners favored the stronger 'neither' reading, much as children do in their first language. This held even when surface word order didn't match the native language, and it was stronger in less proficient learners, which points to shared strategies across first and second language learning.
papers.abstract: A fundamental question in language acquisition is how learners balance input and prior knowledge to infer meaning. Here, we present novel evidence about the mechanisms guiding adults' second language learning. We examined their interpretation of disjunction ("or") in negative sentences (e.g., "John didn't eat the cucumber or the pepper") as a test case. Languages vary in the assignment of scope to logical operators such as negation and disjunction, depending on their syntactic relationship. When multiple interpretations are possible, how do learners assign meaning? Does the native language of L2 learners influence this process? We report three key findings. First, native speakers of Mandarin and Spanish prefer an interpretation where "or" scopes over negation, meaning "John ate either the cucumber or the pepper, but not both" (the "not both" superset interpretation), whereas L2 learners from both backgrounds favor the opposite, subset (stronger) interpretation, where "John ate neither vegetable" (the "neither" subset interpretation). This pattern resembles child first language acquisition. Second, this preference persists even when the surface order of negation and disjunction does not match the native speaker's preferred interpretation, indicating that learners reconstruct underlying structure during interpretation, rather than rely on surface cues. Third, this tendency is stronger in less proficient learners and shifts with increasing proficiency. These findings suggest that L2 learners employ strategies similar to those of children acquiring their first language, initially favoring the stronger possible interpretation. These results shed new light on universal mechanisms guiding both first and second language acquisition.

papers.title: Unpacking the dynamics of cross-situational word learning strategies through trial-by-trial analysis: effects of word frequency distribution and learning context
papers.authors: Zihan Yin, Yujing Shi, Yanli Huang et al.
papers.summary: Across four experiments with adults, the researchers looked at how word frequency distributions affect learning word meanings from co-occurrences across situations. Zipfian distributions, where a few words are very frequent, helped through mutual exclusivity (known mappings help disambiguate new words), especially under high within-trial ambiguity, and their help for associative learning needed high contextual diversity. These trial-by-trial results fed into a model in which the effects of Zipfian input and the mix of learning mechanisms depend on the learning context.
papers.abstract: Word learning in natural environments often relies on cross-situational word learning (CSWL), whereby learners acquire word meanings from word-referent co-occurrences across different situations. Natural language follows Zipfian distributions where a few words occur very frequently while most occur rarely. However, how Zipfian distributions affect CSWL and how learning mechanisms vary across different contexts remain unclear. We addressed these questions in four CSWL experiments with adults. Experiments 1 (N = 36) and 2 (N = 38) found that Zipfian distributions may promote CSWL performance through prospective mutual exclusivity, whereby established mappings support the incremental disambiguation of new words, suggesting that the effectiveness of mutual exclusivity depends on contextual knowledge. Experiments 3 (N = 32) and 4 (N = 42) used trial-by-trial analyses to examine learning mechanisms under Zipfian and uniform distributions across varying levels of within-trial situational ambiguity, randomization, and contextual diversity. The Zipfian advantage emerged under high within-trial ambiguity, while its facilitative effect on associative learning required high contextual diversity. Moreover, hypothesis testing reduced reliance on associative learning under low within-trial ambiguity but enhanced it under high ambiguity. Together, these findings informed the Contextually Modulated Integrative Model of CSWL, in which the effects of Zipfian distributions and the interplay among learning mechanisms depend on learning context. The present study further advances the integrative model of CSWL and clarifies the sources of the Zipfian advantage.

papers.title: Individual differences in spillover during naturalistic reading
papers.authors: Cui Ding, Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox, Lena A. Jäger
papers.summary: Spillover, where a previous word's difficulty carries into reading the current one, shows mixed results at the population level. Analyzing six eye-tracking datasets with Bayesian hierarchical models, the researchers found it differs systematically across readers: less fluent readers show more spillover from word length and frequency, and more fluent readers show more from surprisal. Spillover also related to skipping and regression rates. That suggests averages can hide different reader profiles, which may explain the mixed findings.
papers.abstract: Spillover---the influence of previous words on the processing of current words---is widely reported in reading studies, yet population-level findings are mixed. We argue that spillover is neither noise nor a uniform phenomenon; it may reflect systematic individual differences in how processing difficulty carries over across words. We analyze six naturalistic eye-tracking-while-reading datasets and estimate individual-level spillover effects of preceding-word length, frequency, and surprisal using Bayesian hierarchical models. Because studying individual differences requires reliable measurement, we first assess the cross-context reliability of these effects across experimental sessions and reading tasks, operationalized as correlations between individual-level estimates from two measurement contexts. The measured reliability differs across sources and depends on experimental design and signal-to-noise ratio, being strongest for word length and weaker for lexical frequency and surprisal. Crucially, we find that individual differences in spillover vary systematically with reading fluency. Low-fluency readers exhibit greater spillover from low-level lexical properties, such as word length and frequency, whereas high-fluency readers show more pronounced spillover from higher-level contextual difficulty, such as surprisal, which may help explain why population-level spillover findings are mixed. Finally, spillover is related to skipping and regression rates, indicating that some spillover effects may reflect idiosyncratic patterns of gaze behavior. Overall, our findings suggest that population-level effects can obscure divergent reader profiles, motivating theories and models of reading beyond the "average reader".

papers.title: How semantic seeds shape what can be learned from the input: Evidence for semantic generalization over distributional categories
papers.authors: Abigail Laver, Heesu Yun, Junyi Chen et al.
papers.summary: Adults first learned meanings for a few 'seed' pseudowords, or only their forms, and then heard an artificial language containing seeds and new words. Learners with meaningful seeds developed semantic expectations for new words based on their distributional category, and the expectations vanished when seed meanings and categories were misaligned. Those expectations didn't reliably speed up learning specific word-referent mappings, and learning the distributional structure itself didn't need meaningful seeds. A few known meanings can thus reveal what a distributional category is about.
papers.abstract: Early in language learning, learners may know the meanings of only a small subset of the words they encounter. We refer to these meaningful words as semantic seeds. In three experiments, we asked how this sparse semantic knowledge shapes what learners extract from distributional experience and whether the resulting semantic expectations facilitate word learning. Adults were first introduced to Seed pseudowords. Half of participants learned meanings for these Seeds, whereas the other half were only familiarized with Seed forms. All participants were then exposed to an artificial language with Subject-Object-Verb-like structure, containing Seed and additional, novel Test pseudowords. In Experiments 1a and 1b, learners with meaningful Seeds developed category-consistent semantic expectations for previously meaningless Test words based on their distributional histories. These expectations depended on systematic alignment between Seed meanings and distributional categories: disrupting that alignment eliminated the corresponding semantic preferences. However, these expectations did not reliably accelerate subsequent cross-situational learning of specific word-referent mappings. Experiment 2 showed that Seed meanings generalized to Test words that had never directly co-occurred with Seeds, indicating that semantic properties became associated with distributionally defined categories and were propagated throughout the language. While meaningful Seeds affected the semantic interpretation of distributional categories, they did not affect the acquisition of distributional structure itself; distributional category learning occurred even when Seeds were meaningless. Together, these findings suggest that although learners can acquire distributional structure without semantic knowledge, sparse word meanings can reveal semantic properties of that structure and support meaning hypotheses for otherwise unfamiliar words.

papers.title: Longer cue duration supports stable spatial gradients in multiple-cue inhibition of return
papers.authors: Alfred Lim, Natasha K.Y. Sia, Steve M.J. Janssen et al.
papers.summary: Earlier work found that when several cues appear at once, inhibition of return can organize around the center of gravity of the cue array, but a study with brief 50-ms cues didn't find it persisting. Here, 200-ms cues were tested at 400 and 1000 ms cue-target intervals while measuring saccadic reaction times. Reaction times dropped as targets got farther from the array's center of gravity, particularly for cued targets, at both intervals. Model comparisons couldn't separate center-of-gravity distance from local distance, but the results fit cue duration being an important factor in sustained inhibition.
papers.abstract: When multiple cues are presented simultaneously, inhibitory orienting effects can become organized around the center of gravity (CoG) of the cue array rather than individual cue locations. However, recent work using brief 50-ms cues found that this CoG-organized inhibition of return (IOR) was attenuated at longer cue-target intervals and failed to emerge even in single-cue conditions (Christie et al., 2021), leaving open whether cue duration contributes to durable, spatially organized inhibitory tagging. Here, we tested this possibility using 200-ms cues (the duration used in prior work establishing the CoG effect) across cue-target onset asynchronies (CTOAs) of 400 and 1000 ms, while recording saccadic reaction times (SRTs) in a multiple-cueing task. The 400-ms CTOA replicated conditions known to produce robust CoG effects, and the 1000-ms CTOA provided the novel empirical test. SRT decreased as the distance between the target and the cue-array CoG increased, particularly for cued targets, with CoG-related gradients evident at both CTOAs. Model comparisons on uncued trials indicated that neither CoG distance nor local distance independently accounted for a significant share of variance, suggesting that their relative contributions cannot be separated with the present dataset. These findings are consistent with cue duration being an important parameter in sustained, spatially organized IOR in multiple-cue displays.

papers.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
papers.authors: Sofie Vettori, Farzad Rostami, Jean-Rémy Hochmann et al.
papers.summary: Using frequency-tagging EEG with rapid image streams, the researchers asked whether the brain automatically picks up relations like support (a book on a table) and containment, compared with objects just side by side. Responses were enhanced for relations when they were shown with different exemplars of the same scene, but not when they involved different scenes with distinct object categories. They conclude that relations are not stored as abstract tokens like 'on' or 'in' but as properties tied to the particular objects involved.
papers.abstract: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens ("in" or "on") but rather as objects' properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Stronger mnemonic prediction errors can disproportionately impair memory updating in older adults.
papers.authors: Min Sung Seo, Christopher N. Wahlheim, Kelly S. Giovanello
papers.summary: Younger and older adults studied three-word sequences from one category, shown once or four times, and then saw sequences either repeated or with the last word changed, with the first two words later serving as recall cues for the changed ending. Stronger predictions hurt memory for the changed endings more in older adults, who were also worse at recollecting that an ending had changed. Whenever people did recollect the change, memory for the new ending was better. This suggests strong predictions worsen proactive interference, which is often harder to resolve with age.
papers.abstract: Mnemonic prediction errors are discrepancies between memory-based expectations and actualevents that can trigger memory updating. However, the conditions under which these predictionerrors result in successful memory updating, and whether these effects vary between younger andolder adults, remain less understood. In two experiments, the present study investigated howprediction strength affects memory for events that violated memory-based expectations inyounger and older adults. Prediction strength was manipulated by first presenting three-wordsequences (i.e., trains), each with exemplars from the same category (Bluejay–Hawk–Eagle),either once or four times. Predictions based on memory for trains were then confirmed byrepeating sequences entirely (Bluejay–Hawk–Eagle) or violated by repeating the first two wordsand changing the ending word (Bluejay–Hawk–Robin). Differences in prediction strength,created by varying repetitions, were validated using retrospective judgments (Experiment 1) andprospective predictions of original train endings along with confidence ratings (Experiment 2).Prediction error effects on memory updating were assessed by presenting the first two words oftrains as cues for recalling changed ending words. Stronger predictions impaired memory forchanged endings disproportionately for older adults, and older adults were less able to recollectthat endings had changed when asked directly. Regardless of prediction strength and age, changerecollection was consistently associated with better memory for changed ending words.Collectively, these findings suggest that stronger mnemonic predictions exacerbate the negativeimpact of prediction errors on the resolution of proactive interference, an ability that is oftenimpaired in healthy aging.

papers.title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report.
papers.authors: Hannah Tarder-Stoll, Margaret L. Schlichting, Katherine D. Duncan
papers.summary: In this online registered report, the authors tested whether reward retroactively boosts memory for earlier neutral events, expecting the effect only after a delay and more for associative memory than for item recognition. The planned analyses found no retroactive reward effects on either memory type. Exploratory analyses of people who were behaviorally sensitive to reward, as measured by a separate task, did show delay-dependent enhancement of associative but not item memory. That is suggestive, but it comes from exploratory rather than confirmatory tests.
papers.abstract: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people's memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition-a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative-but not item-memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges.
