papers.title: Listeners expect grammatical variation across dialects.
papers.authors: Zachary K. Maher, Jan Edwards, Charlotte Vaughn et al.
papers.summary: Participants rated how likely a speaker of a given dialect would be to say sentences like "They was happy" versus "He were happy," and then transcribed audio where verb agreement was acoustically ambiguous. Everyone knew African American Language's regularized agreement pattern, but bidialectal speakers of that dialect and Dominant American English showed sharper distinctions, and all listeners heard more regularized agreement when the speaker used African American Language. The effect seemed to follow grammatical cues rather than cues to the speaker's race, which suggests listeners build dialect-specific models of grammar, with precision that depends on their experience.
papers.abstract: Dialect variation is universally attested among languages, yet the cognitive processes underlying listeners' adaptations to different dialects, particularly in morphosyntactic variation, remain underexplored. This article investigates how listeners represent and adapt to their interlocutor's dialect based on their linguistic experience, examining monodialectal speakers of Dominant American English and bidialectal speakers of Dominant American English and African American Language. In Experiment 1, participants rated written sentences to indicate the likelihood that a speaker of a given dialect would say them. All participants demonstrated knowledge of African American Language's regularized subject-verb agreement rules, rating sentences like "They was happy" as more likely than "He were happy." However, bidialectal participants showed greater differentiation between the sentences than monodialectal participants. This finding suggests that listeners do not simply relax grammatical expectations when exposed to linguistic diversity; rather, they form specific expectations of a dialect's grammatical rules. In Experiment 2, we tested whether these expectations influence perception. Participants transcribed sentences where agreement was acoustically ambiguous ("She sit[s] still"). Participants were more likely to transcribe regularized subject-verb agreement ("She sit still") when listening to an African American Language speaker compared to a Dominant American English speaker, regardless of their linguistic experience. Bidialectal participants were more likely to transcribe regularized subject-verb agreement overall. In Experiment 3, we found that such effect patterns were likely driven by morphosyntactic cues, rather than social cues to the race of the speaker. These results suggest that listeners form mental models of others' grammars to guide comprehension, with the precision of these models depending on their linguistic experience. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Dissociation between spontaneous gaze shifts and the spatial coding of number magnitude: Evidence from four high-resolution eye-tracking experiments.
papers.authors: Sara Lo Presti, Marika Mauti, Silvana Lozito et al.
papers.summary: The idea that thinking about small versus large numbers automatically nudges your gaze left or right got a hard test here: across four high-resolution eye-tracking experiments, people judged the magnitude of spoken numbers and showed no magnitude-related gaze shifts, even with a blank screen, a Hermann grid, or landscapes. When participants were explicitly asked to map magnitude onto spatial responses, the usual space-number effect did show up in their responses, but their eyes still didn't move accordingly. The pattern points to spatial-numerical associations arising from the task's response demands rather than being built into number representation.
papers.abstract: Does the brain representation of number magnitude inherently involve space? Early studies suggested that merely perceiving or judging numbers automatically shifts attention and gaze leftward for small numbers and rightward for large ones, supporting the existence of an inherent space-number association. More recent evidence, however, has challenged this view, indicating that spatial-numerical effects arise primarily when spatial and magnitude codes are jointly engaged for response selection. Across four high-resolution eye-tracking experiments, we tested whether discriminating the magnitude of spoken number words elicits overt oculomotor gaze shifts. In Experiments 1-3, participants made verbal magnitude judgments to auditorily presented number words (1-9, excluding 5) while viewing a blank screen (Experiment 1), a Hermann grid designed to facilitate eye movements (Experiment 2), or horizontally symmetrical landscapes presented with or without lateral distractors (Experiment 3). Across all conditions, we found no evidence of horizontal or vertical gaze shifts associated with number magnitude. In Experiment 4, participants explicitly mapped magnitude judgments onto spatial response codes, producing a space-number association of response codes effect. Nevertheless, no spontaneous magnitude-congruent gaze shifts emerged. These findings indicate that number magnitude does not inherently trigger spatially directed eye movements and that spatial-numerical associations depend on task-driven recruitment of both magnitude and spatial response codes. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Does the reading brain possess top-down connections from morphemes to letters?
papers.authors: Maša Mlinarič, Jonathan Grainger, Elisabeth Beyersmann et al.
papers.summary: If morphemes (like the French prefix 'co-') help you see their letters, then letters inside an affix should be easier to identify than the same letters in a non-affix, similar to the classic word superiority effect. In two experiments with 100 French participants each, using free recall and a two-alternative forced-choice task, there was no such advantage. The frequency of the surrounding letter chunks did matter, so the brain seems to learn letter combinations but, here at least, shows no sign of top-down feedback from morphemes.
papers.abstract: No psycholinguist will contradict the importance of morphemes in language processing. But as a cognitive construct, the morpheme and its operations are not fully mapped out yet. Here, we investigated whether morphemes provide top-down support for their constituent letters: a so-called morpheme superiority effect. In two experiments ( N = 100 per experiment), French participants identified single letters in nonword strings that either comprised a French affix (e.g., ‘o’ in ‘ co juste’) or not (‘o’ in ‘ so juste’). In Experiment 1 participants provided free-recall responses by typing letters seen at postcued locations. Experiment 2 was a Reicher–Wheeler (i.e., two-alternative forced-choice) version of the same task. Neither experiment evidenced better identification of target letters embedded in affixes than nonaffixes. On the other hand, we did observe an impact of the frequencies of embedding N-grams (i.e., letter chunks). Hence, while the brain learns and represents letter combinations, we did not observe evidence for morpheme representations partaking in the brain’s feedback loop. Findings are discussed in light of the recent PONG model of word recognition.

papers.title: Phasic alertness: Do warning tones exacerbate interference from salient distractors?
papers.authors: Mei-Ching Lien, Samantha Barondyck, Yuna Lee et al.
papers.summary: An earlier finding suggested that a warning tone widens attention and makes people more vulnerable to salient distractors, but that result hasn't always replicated. Here, the researchers tested it with a visual search task in which a colorful singleton distractor either stood out or was one of three similar distractors. The tone sped up search overall, but it didn't increase capture by the salient distractor, even when the singleton was made task-relevant. That's reassuring for real-world alerts, since the supposed downside didn't appear.
papers.abstract: Using a global/local processing task, Weinbach and Henik (Cognition 133 (2), 414-419, 2014) found that an alerting tone modulated attentional bias for salient stimuli, increasing interference when they were irrelevant to the task. They proposed that phasic alertness broadens attentional focus, increasing one's susceptibility to salient distractors. However, Han and Proctor (2023) failed to replicate their finding using the same task. Here we approached this question with a different paradigm that is commonly used to assess capture by salient color singletons. Specifically, we asked whether phasic alertness amplifies attention capture by salient color singletons. In Experiment 1, participants searched for a predefined target shape among five heterogeneous shapes, which sometimes contained irrelevant colored distractors. The critical manipulation was whether the colored distractor was salient (one irrelevant colored distractor; a singleton) or non-salient (three irrelevant colored distractors; a triplet). The alerting tone was present prior to the search display on half of the trials. Although alerting generally sped up target search, alerting did not increase capture by irrelevant color singletons compared to triplets. Similar results were obtained in Experiment 2 when we promoted capture by the salient color singleton by making it task relevant. Contrary to the saliency-based phasic alertness account, we found no evidence that alerting makes people more susceptible to being captured by salient distractors. PUBLIC SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENTS: Warning tones are often used in real-world contexts to alert users that some task needs to be performed. Understanding how they affect our performance is important for improving safety. Previous studies have suggested that warning tones not only prepare us to do the task but can also have a negative side effect. They may bias our attention to unique but irrelevant salient distractors, increasing their ability to disrupt task performance. However, our study suggests that this negative side effect does not always occur. We found no evidence that an alerting tone increased susceptibility to capture by salient distractors.

papers.title: A registered report on interruptions during visual search: Examining the effects of perceptual and cognitive load
papers.authors: Emily Seeligmüller, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Jan Philipp Röer
papers.summary: Being interrupted mid-search hurts performance, but it's unclear whether a harder interruption does more damage because it's visually harder or because it's more mentally demanding. This preregistered study separates the two: during a running memory span interruption, digits were either clear or masked with visual noise (perceptual load), and people recalled either the last item or the last four (cognitive load). The goal is to see whether the two kinds of load add up and whether one matters more. The abstract describes the design and aims rather than reporting results.
papers.abstract: Interruptions during visual search tasks significantly impair search performance, leading to prolonged reaction time (RT) and reduced accuracy. The interruption’s complexity has been proposed as one important factor that might modulate this decline in performance. However, previous research on interruption complexity during visual search has not clearly differentiated between perceptual and cognitive load, making it difficult to evaluate their relative contributions. This preregistered study examines the effects of interruption complexity on visual search performance by independently manipulating perceptual and cognitive load. Participants performed a visual search task interrupted by a running memory span task. During the interruption task, numerical items were either clearly visible (low perceptual load) or masked with Gaussian visual noise (high perceptual load), and participants recalled either the last item (low cognitive load) or the last four items of the list (high cognitive load). We investigated whether perceptual and cognitive effects are additive and whether one factor is more potent than the other. The results advance theoretical knowledge and contribute to a clearer understanding of the underlying mechanisms of interruption-related performance costs.

papers.title: The role of inhibition in task switching: Evidence from an n-back task
papers.authors: Bihua Cao, Gege Liu, Meiling Fu et al.
papers.summary: To probe how inhibition contributes to task switching, the researchers embedded an n-back task in a magnitude/parity switching paradigm. Switch costs were smaller in the 2-back condition, which demands more inhibition, than in the 1-back condition, and boosting inhibition on selected trials or carrying it over also cut switch costs. The authors read this as evidence that stronger inhibition of irrelevant information makes switching easier, which is a bit counterintuitive.
papers.abstract: Task switching is a well-established paradigm for assessing cognitive flexibility. However, the precise role of inhibition in task switching remains unclear. This study investigates the effects of inhibition on switch costs in tasks requiring participants to judge whether the magnitude (small vs. large) or parity (odd vs. even) of a number was the same as that presented in previous trials. To this end, an n-back task was embedded in the task-switching paradigm. The results of Experiment 1 demonstrated that, in comparison to the 1-back condition, switch costs were significantly reduced in the 2-back condition, which involved an increased inhibition process. The selective increase in inhibition in some trials in the 1-back condition (Experiment 2) and the carryover of inhibition (Experiment 3) significantly reduced the switch costs. These findings indicate that the enhanced inhibition of task-irrelevant information can facilitate cognitive flexibility in task switching and reduce switch costs, providing novel empirical evidence for the inhibition mechanism underlying task switching.

papers.title: Viewers Actively Extract and Maintain Spontaneous Theory of Mind Representations in Dramatic Irony Scenes
papers.authors: Cynthia Cabañas, Sam Boland, Atsushi Senju et al.
papers.summary: Dramatic irony, where viewers know something a character doesn't, offers a natural way to study how people track other minds. Participants watched Harold Lloyd silent film clips, either as self-paced frames or as full video, while their eyes were tracked. When viewers held privileged information, so the character had a false belief, they looked longer at moments of conflict and showed longer fixations, and in the video version also fewer fixations and smaller saccades. This suggests viewers spontaneously build and hold onto false-belief representations as they watch.
papers.abstract: Understanding others’ mental states is a cornerstone of human cognition, yet how spontaneous belief attribution operates in complex, naturalistic perception remains underexplored. Dramatic irony (DI)—a narrative device through which viewers are aware of information unknown to characters—provides a controlled but naturalistic context to examine these processes. Using a curated DI film corpus, we combined eye‐tracking with (a) self‐paced and (b) video viewing to investigate how Spontaneous Theory of Mind shapes real‐time processing. Across two experiments, participants viewed edited Harold Lloyd silent film excerpts that either provided privileged information (Installation condition) or aligned viewer and character knowledge (Control condition), reflecting false‐ and true‐belief scenarios. Clips were either presented as a self‐paced static series of frames (Experiment 1) or dynamic film clips (Experiment 2). We analyzed narrative comprehension, reaction times, and eye‐tracking measures indexing cognitive effort. Results showed that, relative to the Control condition, the Installation condition yielded longer viewing times at moments of representational conflict, indicating increased cognitive demands associated with maintaining and applying false‐belief representations. In Experiment 1, these effects emerged at discrete moments and were accompanied by longer fixation durations in the Installation condition. In Experiment 2, longer fixation durations in the Installation condition were again observed, alongside reduced fixation rates and saccade amplitudes, consistent with more sustained local processing. These findings indicate that viewers spontaneously construct and maintain false‐belief representations during DI, which modulate real‐time processing during scene comprehension, providing a tractable framework for investigating social reasoning in dynamic visual contexts.

papers.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
papers.authors: Zach Paris, Emily Finn
papers.summary: Using reduced-rank regression, the researchers asked which parts of a language model's internal representations actually predict brain activity during naturalistic listening, across intracranial and fMRI datasets. Just 1-3% of the embedding dimensions were enough to recover full predictive performance, and these subspaces generalized across participants and somewhat across datasets. Those brain-relevant directions differ from the ones that capture the most variance in the model, so brain alignment seems to live in a small, structured slice of the representation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

papers.title: Local learning is all you need: brain-aligned predictive coding networks
papers.authors: Dirk Gütlin, Ryszard Auksztulewicz, Adrien Doerig
papers.summary: Predictive coding models have been biologically appealing but have lagged behind standard deep networks in performance and in matching the brain. The researchers introduce Predictive Brain Networks, a hierarchical recurrent model trained with local, predictive-coding-style learning, which matches or beats established vision models in alignment with the human ventral visual stream. It also beats other predictive-coding-inspired networks on classification, reproduces signatures like higher-level predictions shaping lower-level responses, and supports uncertainty estimation, suggesting local learning doesn't have to cost representational power.
papers.abstract: Predictive Coding (PC) is an influential account of how brain representations emerge through hierarchical, local, self-supervised prediction-based learning, without requiring globally propagated error signals. Despite extensive evidence supporting PC, a striking paradox persists: computational models built on these biologically grounded principles have consistently failed to match state-of-the-art Deep Neural Networks in performance and brain-alignment. Here, we show that this paradox can be overcome. We introduce Predictive Brain Networks (PBNs), a hierarchical recurrent framework that implements local PC-based learning and achieves representational alignment with the human ventral visual stream matching or exceeding established vision models. Importantly, PBN top-down predictions encode unique, brain-aligned information not captured during bottom-up feature extraction, with this contribution increasing in locally trained variants. Further, PBNs substantially outperform existing PC-inspired networks on downstream classification tasks, reproduce key signatures of PC (with higher-level predictions shaping lower-level visual responses as observed in the primate cortex), and support uncertainty estimation. PBNs therefore close a longstanding gap in computational neuroscience by combining two properties that have been largely separated: the brain-inspired learning mechanisms of predictive coding and the representational power of modern deep networks. They provide a scalable framework for studying biologically grounded learning without sacrificing the capacity to produce rich neural representations.

papers.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments
papers.authors: Kianté Fernandez, Caitlin Chen, Jialu Zhou et al.
papers.summary: Most tests of language models' cognitive abilities use text prompts, which skip the visual interfaces and time pressure human participants face. CogArena instead has multimodal agents complete ten behavioral experiments through a regular web browser, scoring whether they finished, how accurately they performed, and whether their data show the usual human behavioral signatures. Across four models, many sessions didn't finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. The benchmark is public with a leaderboard, and it's relevant to worries about AI agents contaminating online datasets.
papers.abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.

papers.title: Children’s quantification of time with the comparative “more”
papers.authors: Kosta Boskovic, David Barner
papers.summary: Asking 'Who did more walking?' requires picking duration as the dimension and comparing the amounts, which could be harder than comparing number or space. In three studies, children judged who did more of an action when two actors performed it for different durations. By age 3 or 4 they could do it, years before they learn words like 'minute' and 'hour', and about when they manage the same comparison for number and space.
papers.abstract: Events can be quantified along several dimensions— E.g., walking can be measured by number of steps taken, distance traveled, or time spent walking. In quantifying events with the comparative “more” (e.g., “Who did more walking?”), one must first identify the relevant dimension of quantification and encode each magnitude, before projecting them onto a common scale of degrees to support linguistic comparison. In the current study, we asked whether young children are able to do so for duration, which may be less salient than number or space. While previous work has established that children quantify number and space with “more” by 3 ½ years old, it is unknown whether children are able to quantify duration around this age, or whether this ability emerges later in development, perhaps closer to when children learn duration words such as “minute” and “hour” around 6 or 7 years old. In three studies, we asked children to identify who did “more” of an action (e.g., stretching) performed by two actors for varying durations. We found that children could quantify duration with “more” by 3 or 4 years old. These results suggest that children can identify time as the relevant dimension of quantification and encode a comparison of the magnitude of durations linguistically years before mastering duration words, and around when they become able to quantify magnitudes in more concrete domains such as number and space.

papers.title: Novelty Processing in Aging: Absence of an Association with Episodic Memory Abilities
papers.authors: Anaïs Servais, Christine Bastin
papers.summary: Seventy-eight older adults completed eye-tracking and pupillometry tasks measuring how much they're drawn to novel items, either completely unknown ones or new arrangements of familiar elements, and the researchers correlated these with episodic memory performance. Participants showed reliable novelty preferences, but these were mostly unrelated to memory scores, with only a few unexpected links to verbal recall. Compared with younger adults, gaze-based novelty preferences looked similar, though pupil dilation to novelty was smaller in older adults, which suggests novelty processing is largely independent of episodic memory and may hold up with age.
papers.abstract: Conceptually, novelty processing and episodic memory are closely linked. Yet it remains unclear whether they rely on common or partly independent mechanisms. We investigated whether their relationship depends on the type of novelty and representational content in healthy older adults. Seventy-eight adults aged 61–84 years completed eye-tracking tasks assessing Absolute novelty (unknown stimuli) and Associative novelty (novel configurations of familiar elements) for objects and scenes, as well as a pupillometry task assessing responses to novel objects. Novelty-processing indices were correlated with performance across various episodic memory tasks using preregistered Bayesian correlations. Older adults showed reliable gaze preferences for both Absolute and Associative novelty in object and scene tasks. Contrary to our predictions, however, Absolute novelty preference was generally unrelated to performance on familiarity-based recognition and perceptual discrimination measures hypothesized to rely on the perirhinal cortex. Associative novelty preference was likewise largely unrelated to episodic memory performance, although a small number of unexpected associations with verbal recall emerged for object novelty. Novelty-related pupil responses also showed little evidence of associations with memory performance. Exploratory comparisons with data from younger adults aged 18-30 years (from Servais &amp; Bastin, 2026) indicated largely comparable gaze-based novelty preferences across age groups, although novelty-related peak pupil dilation was reduced in older adults. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in novelty processing, when assessed in paradigms with no memory confound, are largely independent of episodic memory performance in healthy older adults and that gaze-based novelty processing may remain preserved with age for both novelty types.

papers.title: Which memory does brain stimulation improve? The priming problem
papers.authors: Halil Aziz Velioglu, murat can çelik, Dogukan Aslan et al.
papers.summary: Brain stimulation studies show boosts on episodic memory tests, and these are usually read as better intentional retrieval. This narrative review argues that repetition priming, which makes repeated items easier to process, can raise recognition and cued-recall scores even if retrieval itself hasn't changed, and TMS can also affect priming directly. Since nobody has estimated how much priming contributes to the gains, the authors propose five measurement steps, centered on matched indirect tests and process-dissociation procedures, that could be used in clinical trials.
papers.abstract: Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of cortical sites connected with the hippocampus improves scores on episodic memory tests and is being tested for memory decline, including in Alzheimer's disease. These gains are read as gains in intentional retrieval. Objective: To examine whether standard memory outcomes can support this reading and how the contribution of repetition priming can be measured. Methods: Narrative review of hippocampal-network stimulation studies, cognitive and electrophysiological research on priming and processing fluency, stimulation studies of priming and parietal cortex, and clinical trials of TMS for memory decline. Results: Old/new recognition and cued recall present studied items or cues again at test. Repetition priming makes these items easier to process, and this fluency can raise a memory score with intentional retrieval unchanged. The fluency behind word-recognition decisions is largely conceptual, so it persists after a change of surface form. TMS can also alter priming directly, and stimulating the standard parietal target changes the subjective side of recollection. Meta-analytic evidence shows that the gains are specific to episodic memory and largest for recollection tests after stimulation before encoding, but the priming contribution to these gains has not been estimated. Conclusions: Process-level claims about stimulation-related memory gains require the priming contribution to be measured. Five measurement steps, centred on matched indirect tests and process-dissociation procedures, make it measurable in the same participants, including in clinical trials.

papers.title: Persistent Belief Updating Despite Perfect Predictability – The Atypical Iterative Prior Updating Account Of Autism
papers.authors: Yun Wai Foo, Sonja Coenen, Christine Falter-Wagner et al.
papers.summary: This proposal, the atypical iterative prior updating account, holds that in autism the difference lies in how beliefs get updated over time, with sensory evidence overweighted, rather than in forming priors or weighting prediction errors. Autistic and typically developing adults did a distractor suppression task with a perfectly valid cue while their eye movements were tracked. Both groups showed the same first-fixation capture, but autistic participants had more interference, more fixations, and more target refixations that emerged after initial selection. The authors interpret this as continued evidence sampling even when the outcome is fully predictable.
papers.abstract: Background: Within predictive coding accounts of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), two competing explanations locate perceptual atypicalities within inference: weak prior formation versus altered weighting of prediction errors. We propose the atypical iterative prior updating (AIPU) account, which shifts the locus from inference to what happens afterwards: sensory evidence is overweighted during iterative belief updating over time. The accounts predict distinct temporal signatures of attentional divergence. Methods: To distinguish among the accounts, we presented autistic and typically developing adults with a distractor suppression paradigm using a 100%-valid spatial cue and varying distractor prevalence, while eye movements tracked the temporal dynamics of attentional selection. Results: Both groups showed equivalent first-fixation capture, ruling out prior-formation differences. Distractor prevalence modulated interference differently across groups. Autistic participants produced larger reaction time interference, more fixations, and more target refixations, a pattern emerging after initial selection. These findings locate ASD-related differences specifically in iterative updating across time, not in perceptual inference. Conclusions: The mechanism points to sustained attentional engagement: rather than terminating sensory sampling once expectations are confirmed, autistic individuals continue accumulating evidence even under perfect predictability. The world might feel "too much" not because perceptual inference is altered, but because updating continues beyond resolution.

papers.title: When children choose not to know: The development of deliberate ignorance
papers.authors: Linda Kerbl, Zoe Rahwan, Ralph Hertwig et al.
papers.summary: Do kids ever choose not to know something, like not opening a present early or not listening in on a tense conversation? In 13 vignettes given to 150 children aged 6-12, children preferred deliberate ignorance in 31% of cases on average, up to 75% for one vignette, and only 8% always chose to know. Preferences for not knowing grew with age and with prior real-world experience of the information, and dropped for outcomes children saw as threatening. It suggests this way of managing information shows up in middle childhood.
papers.abstract: When you were a child, did you tear open presents immediately or wait to savor the surprise? When you heard your parents’ loud voices, did you eavesdrop or retreat, trying not to hear? These everyday moments reflect an important capacity: the ability to decide not to know, even when information is available, potentially relevant, and nearly costless. This phenomenon has been called deliberate ignorance. While deliberate ignorance is well-documented in adults, including in highly consequential domains, such as health or social decisions, little is known about how it develops. Across 13 vignettes we examined preferences for deliberate ignorance in 150 children aged 6 to 12 years. We find that deliberate ignorance exists, already in middle childhood: On average, children preferred deliberate ignorance in 31% of cases; reaching up to 75% in one vignette. Only 8% of children (n = 12) preferred to know across all vignettes. Children with prior real-world experience with the presented information were more likely to prefer not to know, and this preference for deliberate ignorance increased with age. Children preferred ignorance less for outcomes that they perceived as threatening. Our findings offer new insights into early signatures of deliberate ignorance as a tool children use to regulate their information intake as they adapt to increasingly complex information environments with age.

papers.title: Differences in associative change between cues trained in compound are better explained by individual prediction errors than by relative certainty
papers.authors: Amin Jahani, Metin Üngör
papers.summary: Across six human predictive-learning experiments, people learned which foods raised or lowered a patient's inflammation. The researchers then trained excitatory and inhibitory cues together in compound and tested which cue changed more. In four experiments the results fit the idea that cues with larger individual prediction errors change the most, rather than the idea that people shield the cue they're more certain about. One experiment showed the opposite pattern, but it didn't replicate.
papers.abstract: The present experiments investigated associative changes during compound training involving cues with different learning histories. In six human predictive-learning experiments using the compound-test procedure (Rescorla, 2000), participants learned about the effects of foods (cues) on inflammation (outcome) in a hypothetical patient. Each food could cause decreases in inflammation, increases in inflammation, or had no effect. Cues A and C were trained as excitatory, whereas cues B and D were trained to acquire inhibitory properties. Participants then received compound training in which A and B were presented together and followed by an outcome that should produce associative loss, followed by a final test in which outcome expectations were assessed for the test compounds AD and BC. The initial training designs were expected to produce greater relative certainty about A than B, with A generating a larger individual prediction error than B during the compound training. If cues generating larger individual prediction errors undergo greater associative change, AD should receive lower ratings than BC. Alternatively, if participants preferentially attribute the compound outcome to the less certain cue (theory protection), BC should receive lower ratings than AD. Overall, the compound-test results were more consistent with an individual prediction-error account: AD was rated lower than BC in Experiments 1, 2, 5, and 6. Experiment 3 showed the opposite pattern, consistent with theory protection, but this pattern was not replicated in Experiment 4. We discuss the implications of these findings for the roles of prediction error and certainty in associative learning.

papers.title: Age-of-acquisition Effects across the Adult Lifespan: Evidence from Eye Movements in Compound Word Reading
papers.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif, wanyin li, Meyrem Tompson et al.
papers.summary: Words learned early in life are usually recognised faster, and here eye-tracking tested whether that holds for compound words, with and without a space between the parts, in young and older adults. Young readers showed the age-of-acquisition effect for both formats. Older readers showed it only for unspaced compounds, and the effect shrank with age. The authors read this as older readers leaning more on the individual parts of a word when spacing breaks up its visual form.
papers.abstract: The Age of Acquisition (AoA) effect is where words acquired during childhood are recognised more quickly than those acquired during adulthood. However, the influence of AoA on compound words and its stability across the adult lifespan remain under-investigated. We conducted two eye-tracking experiments to clarify how the AoA effect is moderated by ageing and spacing. Ninety British English adults participated across two eye-tracking experiments: 60 young adults (30 reading unspaced compounds in Experiment 1 and 30 reading spaced compounds in Experiment 2) and 30 older adults (who read both unspaced and spaced compounds across experiments). Using Bayesian linear mixed-effects models, we observed a robust AoA effect in both spaced and unspaced compound words in young adults. However, in older adults, we only observed an AoA effect in unspaced compound words. The AoA effect declined with increasing age, whereas the slope of AoA effect was shallower in spaced than unspaced compound words. These findings suggest that the functional influence of AoA is contingent upon orthographic structure and reading experience: while whole-word AoA influences processing across visual formats in younger readers, older readers shift away from whole-word lexical properties toward constituent-level strategies when orthographic structure is disrupted by spacing.

papers.title: Learning and Using Value Maps in Multi-Dimensional Choice
papers.authors: Ata Baris Karagoz, Akram Bakkour
papers.summary: Participants learned three mappings from perceptual features to value, then chose between new composite options while a mouse-contingent display forced them to look at information one piece at a time. People differed a lot in how they read the learned values, from precise 'how much better' comparisons to simple 'which is ahead' ones. Most mixed the two, rather than treating ordinal comparison as a blurry version of the metric one. How well each dimension was learned set its weight in the choice, and the way people read values and weighted dimensions both showed up in their information search.
papers.abstract: When making choices between multi-dimensional options, people draw upon knowledgeof the options’ various properties to make a decision. While much work has probed howindividuals make decisions in these modes, less is known of how learned value maps canbe flexibly composed to support novel decisions. Here we taught participants three separateperceptual-to-value mappings, each dividing a continuous perceptual dimension into five valuecategories. We then had them choose between composite options never encountered duringlearning while a mouse-contingent display forced serial information sampling. How the learnedmap was read during choice varied widely across people, from fully metric reads (e.g. howmuch better) to purely ordinal ones (e.g. which is ahead). We find that ordinal comparison isnot simply a degraded version of the same metric. Instead, participants mix between ordinaland metric reads. How well each dimension was learned set its weight, while how stronglylearning accuracy depended on the separation between categories lowered both the weightsand the metric share of the read. Both the readout and weights left separable signatures ininformation search. Learned value maps are thus composed and then read out to guide choice.

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Experiential and Distributional Representations for Concrete and Abstract Concepts
papers.authors: Laxmi R. Iyer, Martin Takac, Igor Farkas
papers.summary: Comparing human similarity ratings with models built from experiential (grounded) features and from language-based distributional features, this work looked at how concrete and abstract concepts are represented. It found a double dissociation: grounded features line up better with human judgements for concrete concepts, while language-based features do better for abstract ones. Abstract concepts also sit in a compressed, clustered region of experiential space, organised more by how abstract they are than by meaning.
papers.abstract: We investigate the semantic distinction between concrete and abstract concepts byexamining the relative contribution of experiential (grounded) features and distributional(language-based) features in modeling their representation via data driven analysis usingSpearman’s correlation between human similarity ratings, representational similarityanalysis between various feature spaces, multidimensional scaling, and category similarity.Our results reveal a robust double dissociation between feature types and concept classes.Grounded features better align with human judgements for concrete concepts than forabstract concepts. Concrete concepts exhibit higher representational similarity acrossdifferent independently obtained grounded feature representations. In contrast, languagebased features better align with human judgements for abstract concepts than for concreteconcepts. Abstract concepts exhibit higher representational similarity across differentindependently obtained distributional feature representations. Multidimensional scalinganalyses further show that abstract concepts occupy a compressed and highly clusteredregion in experiential space, with clustering driven more by degree of abstractness thansemantic similarity. Concrete concepts in contrast are highly correlated with sensorimotorfeatures in experiential space. Further, better category similarity for concrete concepts isexhibited by experiential features rather than distributional features.

papers.title: Beyond Consequences of Challenge: the Degree to which Spoken Word Recognition Changes in Response to Difficulty has Independent Relevance
papers.authors: John Baltazar Muegge, Bob McMurray
papers.summary: Listeners tracked words with eye movements (the Visual World Paradigm) in two kinds of challenging listening, across two days, and a principal component analysis pulled out the main dimensions of how recognition changes under difficulty. How someone's word recognition shifts under challenge was predicted by how they process speech in quiet, and it stayed stable across days and across types of challenge. The size of that shift also predicted how well they did on speech-in-noise comprehension tests, so it seems to be a meaningful individual trait.
papers.abstract: Listeners must often recognize words in challenging listening conditions like background noise. The cognitive mechanisms of spoken word recognition offer a potential locus for adaptation to such contexts. Indeed, research has found that the millisecond-by-millisecond dynamics of word recognition in challenging conditions differ lawfully along a small number of dimensions. However, comparatively little is known about the factors that impact the nature of an individual listener’s response to challenge. Here we ask if this response is stable across time and challenge type, if it is constrained by the idiosyncrasies of how listeners recognize words in quiet, and if these patterns of processing predict performance in real-world outcome measures. We tested listeners in a Visual World Paradigm with two different types of challenging listening across two days. We then leveraged a principal component analysis to extract underlying dimensions of variance across these conditions. Using this approach, we found that the dynamics of word recognition in challenge are predicted by their dynamics in typical speech, that these dynamics are stable across days and different types of challenge, and that the magnitude with which listeners change recognition predicts their performance in tests of speech-in-noise comprehension.

papers.title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
papers.authors: van Haren, J. J. G., de Lange, F. P., Kotz, S. A. et al.
papers.summary: Using MEG while people listened to tone sequences whose statistics shifted periodically, the researchers tracked prior precision, surprisal, model updating and simple tone adaptation at once. They found a sequence in time: precision of expectations came first, then repetition suppression and surprisal together, then model updates spread across fronto-parietal networks. Each process also had its own oscillatory signature, including theta-alpha for adaptation and beta suppression for surprisal. The picture is of fast local gating and mismatch signals coming before the slower revision of internal models.
papers.abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Yet, how all these concurrent mechanisms unfold in time remains underexplored. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in participants listening to stochastic tone sequences with periodically shifting inferential statistics, we modelled the temporal, spatial, and spectral dynamics of stimulus-specific repetition suppression, surprisal, model updating, and prior precision. By concurrently tracking these computational parameters within this dynamic auditory environment, we revealed a distinct chronological hierarchy governing predictive and adaptive processing. Prior precision states - reflecting expectations - emerged earliest, followed by rapid and concurrent repetition suppression and surprisal - reflecting local acoustic attenuation and global mismatch detection. These initial dynamics culminated in subsequent, distributed model updates within fronto-parietal networks. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

papers.title: Mentalization as a mechanism for constructing meaning under ambiguity
papers.authors: Serena Maria Stagnitto, Celia Martínez-Tomás, Serena Lecce et al.
papers.summary: In this study, 103 participants wrote definitions for real words and pseudowords and completed three mentalization measures. Using representational similarity analysis, the team found that people who described Theory-of-Mind animations (the Triangles task) similarly also defined pseudowords similarly, but not real words. This held even after controlling for how they described control Action clips. The IRI and the Eyes Test showed no such link. The authors suggest that making sense of novel words draws on the same tendencies we use to read social meaning into ambiguous situations.
papers.abstract: Pseudowords lack conventional lexical meanings, but growing evidence suggests that they can nevertheless elicit structured (semantic) interpretations. The present study (N = 103) tested whether individual differences in mentalization are related to how people construct meanings for novel verbal stimuli. Participants generated definitions for real words and pseudowords and completed three mentalization-related measures: the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), and the Triangles task. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we examined whether participants who were similar in mentalization-related profiles were also similar in their definition profiles. IRI and RMET response-profile similarity showed no evidence of an association with definition similarity, while similarity in open-ended descriptions of Triangles Theory-of-Mind animations predicted similarity in pseudoword definitions, but not real-word definitions. This association remained significant after controlling for similarity in Triangles control Action-clip descriptions, suggesting that it was not reducible to shared verbal-response format or general description style. Additional reconstruction analyses showed that pseudoword-definition embeddings can partially recover the participant-level representational geometry of Theory-of-Mind descriptions. These findings suggest that novel meaning construction is not only a lexical-semantic process but is also aligned with broader interpretive tendencies involved in assigning coherent social meaning to ambiguous experience, with implications for understanding the links between semantic cognition, mentalization, and developmental word learning.

papers.title: An ERP Study of the Effects of Category Knowledge and Contextual Knowledge Using a Cue–Target Matching Paradigm
papers.authors: Xiaoying Huang, Binyue Gao, Yoshimichi Ejima et al.
papers.summary: Combining a cue-target matching task with ERPs, this study compared two kinds of prior knowledge in object categorization: category knowledge at three levels of specificity, and contextual knowledge such as typical color and scene. Both kinds affected several processing stages, but with different timing. Category knowledge showed level-dependent effects across intermediate, conflict and later stages, while contextual knowledge mostly modulated the P2 and N400. So different kinds of knowledge appear to help categorization on different timelines.
papers.abstract: Object categorization depends not only on the current visual input but also on prior knowledge. However, whether different types of prior knowledge influence object categorization with the same temporal profile remains unclear. In this study, we combined a cue-target matching paradigm with event-related potentials (ERPs) to compare the effects of category knowledge and contextual knowledge on object categorization. Category knowledge was manipulated at the superordinate, intermediate, and basic levels, whereas contextual knowledge was based on typical color and scene information. The behavioral results showed that cue-target congruency affected task performance, with different patterns observed across cue conditions. The ERP results further revealed that prior knowledge influenced multiple stages of processing, but the temporal pattern varied across conditions. Category knowledge showed level-dependent effects across intermediate, conflict, and later processing stages, whereas contextual knowledge was associated mainly with P2 and N400 modulation. These findings suggest that different types of prior knowledge contribute to object categorization with different temporal dynamics and that these differences may be related to how the relevant information is structured and used during cue-target matching.

papers.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
papers.authors: Mark G. Pillai, Cody A. Mashburn, Jason S. Tsukahara et al.
papers.summary: In 336 participants, pupil dilation was recorded during pitch, duration and loudness discrimination tasks, alongside measures of attention control, working memory and fluid intelligence. Attention control predicted discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the link between pupil dilation and performance. People with strong attention control showed steeper pupil increases as tasks got harder and kept their accuracy. For people with weak attention control, big pupil responses looked more like effort that didn't pay off.
papers.abstract: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition. papers.title: Processing speed, not multitasking, drives expert decision-making under pressure.
papers.authors: Eleanor R. A. Hyde, Robert Schmidt, Daniel J. Carroll et al.
papers.summary: Here, 230 Counter-Strike players were grouped into four expertise levels and tested on processing speed and task switching. Experts had faster reaction times than novices but no specific multitasking advantage. Drift-diffusion modeling traced the speed edge to faster evidence accumulation (higher drift rates) and shorter nondecision time, with no difference in boundary separation, the strategic part of decision-making. Expertise under pressure looks like general speed rather than better multitasking.
papers.abstract: = 230 players (16-34 years) of the video game Counter-Strike into four expertise clusters (Novice, Skilled, Emerging, and Expert), assessing their processing speed and task-switching performance. To better understand the source of expertise effects, we used drift-diffusion modeling to estimate nondecision and decision components of performance. Experts exhibited significantly faster reaction times than Novices, but no specific multitasking advantage was observed. The drift-diffusion modeling revealed that this speed advantage was driven by higher drift rates and shorter nondecision times. No expertise-related differences were found in boundary separation, the strategic component of decision-making. Findings suggest that expert performance in decision-making under pressure is characterized by advantages in general processing speed rather than being associated with greater multitasking capabilities. papers.title: Is the Proust phenomenon fact or fiction? A systematic review and meta-analysis of odor-evoked autobiographical memory
papers.authors: Ovidiu I. Bobei, Dragos Cîrneci, Ioana R. Podina
papers.summary: Is smell really the strongest trigger for autobiographical memories? This meta-analysis pooled 18 studies that compared odor cues with other cue types. Odors beat other cues for emotional intensity, pleasantness, evocativeness and the age of the memories evoked, but not for the other characteristics assessed. Effects varied with study design, sample size and other factors. The authors conclude the Proust phenomenon is real but selective rather than universal.
papers.abstract: Odors are widely believed to be the most powerful trigger for autobiographical memory (AM). This meta-analysis provides the first comprehensive meta-analytic test of this claim, known as the Proust phenomenon. Eighteen experimental/quasi-experimental studies were included in this meta-analysis. Olfactory cueing was compared with a variety of cueing modalities, and seven key characteristics of evoked AMs (specificity, vividness, emotional intensity, pleasantness, rarity, evocativeness, and age of AMs) were assessed. Olfactory cues showed a greater effect (advantage) over other cue types for emotional intensity, pleasantness, evocativeness, and age of AMs. Sample size was negatively associated with effect sizes for emotional intensity, pleasantness, and rarity, although the overall effect for rarity was not significant. Higher proportions of females and more recent publication years were each associated with smaller effects for evocativeness and pleasantness, respectively. Subgroup analyses showed that the advantage of olfactory cues for emotional intensity was stronger in within-subject than between-subject designs. Moreover, their advantage in terms of pleasantness was greatest relative to label cues, followed by visual and auditory cues. Although olfactory cues showed an advantage for four characteristics of AMs, these results do not fully confirm the Proust phenomenon. Overall, these findings suggest that the olfactory advantage is selective rather than universal, and future studies should clarify the conditions under which it emerges.

papers.title: Smart brands, trustworthy people, and evil words: Sub-lexical distributional patterns capture human semantic associations for names and novel words
papers.authors: Joris van Eijkelenburg, Aron Joosse, Erik-Jan van Kesteren et al.
papers.summary: Dutch speakers rated given names, pseudowords and made-up company names on femininity, evilness, smartness and trustworthiness, and all three item types produced robust associations. A model based on sub-lexical patterns (pieces of word form) predicted ratings well for pseudowords. Raters seemed to rely on other information for given names on smartness and trustworthiness, and for company names that departed from typical Dutch sound patterns. The work shows when word form alone can carry meaning and when other sources take over.
papers.abstract: We show that given names, pseudowords, and made-up company names elicit robust associations across four semantic dimensions (femininity, evilness, smartness, and trustworthiness) in a best-worst scaling survey administered to Dutch native speakers. Associations were strongest for semantic dimensions associated with conventional morphological markers (gender, evilness) but did not differ substantially across item types. Critically, items varied in the degree to which they belong in native speakers' linguistic experience: names are experienced, pseudowords and made-up company names are not, but the former were designed to be indistinguishable from Dutch words and thus obey orthotactic constraints, whereas the latter need not. We also used a sub-lexical distributional semantic model to extract an unsupervised metric quantifying the degree of association between a string and a semantic dimension, which we then correlated with human ratings. When reliable sub-lexical patterns were available, participants could exploit them in rating strings (robust correlations for pseudowords on all four target dimensions), but relied on other sources of information both when experience with the full form was available and the semantic dimension was not associated with conventional morphological markers (given names and smartness/trustworthiness), or when strings diverged from typical sub-lexical patterns (made-up company names). These results further characterize the relation between word form and lexical meaning and the mechanisms that support semantic associations for known and novel strings.

papers.title: A crucial source of psychological certainty in human cognition: The certainty signature of central form
papers.authors: Paul Haward
papers.summary: Why do people feel certain about some beliefs? Drawing on Form Theory, this paper tests whether certainty comes from a concept's 'central form', its core structure. When people judged new instances of familiar concepts, they generalized both form and non-form properties but felt certain only about form properties. The same held for newly learned concepts: a property encoded as part of the central form brought much more certainty than the same property introduced in a generic sentence. The authors suggest that conceptual structure is one source of overconfidence.
papers.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept's central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept's central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

papers.title: Countermanding saccades in children
papers.authors: Timothy L. Hodgson, Jonathan Waddington, Kirsten Williams et al.
papers.summary: In the countermanding saccade task, people must sometimes hold back an eye movement when a stop signal appears. 181 primary-school children did child-friendly versions across three experiments. Children often failed to move their eyes even when told to ignore the signal, and the visual stop signal itself produced dips in the reaction time distributions. The authors conclude that the signal has an exogenous inhibitory effect that fades with age, so the task shouldn't be read simply as a measure of developing inhibitory control.
papers.abstract: The countermanding saccade task is a widely used test of reactive inhibitory oculomotor control. The test comprises “Go” trials, in which saccades are directed towards target onsets, interspersed with “Stop” trials, where a signal sometime after target onset indicates that a saccade should be withheld or “countermanded”. Computational models of the task assume a race to threshold between internal go and stop processes, the outcome of which determines whether a programmed response is cancelled. In this study, 181 typically developing primary-school-aged children completed child-friendly versions of the task. Three experiments examined the effect of task instruction (either to countermand saccades or ignore stop signals), stop signal characteristics (with and without an overlapping fixation cue) and practice (one versus two blocks). Children often failed to make saccades even when they were instructed to ignore the signal and make a response to the target on every trial. Saccade reaction times were longer on Stop compared with correct Go trials and significant “dips” (reductions in expected response frequency within discrete time bins) were observed in reaction time distributions associated with the change in the colour of the fixation stimulus that served as a stop signal. It is concluded that visual stop signals exert an exogenous inhibitory effect on saccades which decreases with increasing age. As such, care should be taken in interpreting the oculomotor stop signal task as a straightforward test of developing inhibitory control or the maturation of an internal stop process. Open access statement Experiment task code, raw trial-level data, and analysis files for all experiments are available via the Open Science Framework: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/Q4PGH . The study protocol was not preregistered.

papers.title: Edge structure influences infants’ and toddlers’ engagement with natural scenes
papers.authors: Brianna K. Hunter, Kaitlyn Wong, Lisa M. Oakes
papers.summary: How do edges in a picture affect where babies and toddlers look? Infants (5-12 months) and toddlers (13-21 months) viewed natural scenes that varied in the proportion of horizontal and vertical edges and in the total quantity of edges. Infants looked longer at scenes with more edges and less at scenes with a higher proportion of cardinal edges. Toddlers preferred a moderate proportion of cardinal edges and ignored edge quantity. The influence of these properties also shifted with age within each group.
papers.abstract: Low-level features, or basic visual properties like color, luminance, and orientation, guide visual attention across the lifespan. We evaluated how variations in one low-level feature, edge structure, related to visual attention to natural scenes (i.e., photographs of places such as kitchens and landscapes) across the first two postnatal years of life. Specifically, we asked how the proportion of cardinal edges (i.e., horizontal and vertical) as well as the edge quantity within scenes related to infants’ ( N = 107, 5 to 12 months; 63 girls and 44 boys, 39.25% were White and not Hispanic, and the remaining infants were Asian, Black, Multiracial, and/or Hispanic) and toddlers’ ( N = 79, 13 to 21 months; 39 girls, 39 boys, 1 not reported, 45.57% were White and not Hispanic, and the remaining toddlers were Asian, Black, Multiracial, and/or Hispanic) visual attention to those scenes. We found that infants looked longer at scenes with more edges and decreased their looking to scenes with a higher proportion of cardinal edges. In contrast, toddlers looked longer at scenes with a moderate proportion of cardinal edges, and their looking was unrelated to edge quantity. Within both samples, we found that the role of these edge properties changed with age. Therefore, there appear to be developmental changes from infancy to toddlerhood in the role of edge structure on children’s attention to natural scenes. Open practices statement Materials that support the findings of this study are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/zdghu ). We provide fixation data for both experiments, analysis code, and experiment stimuli. Experiments were not preregistered.
